record.original_question: Given a Diophantine equation, determine whether it has at least one integer solution.

evidence.quote: Maybe the most famous question about Diophantine equations is Hilbert 10th problem:
Problem 6. Given a Diophantine equation, determine whether it has an integer solution.

artifact.self_contained_problem: A Diophantine equation is an equation of the form $P(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n) = 0$, where $P \in \mathbb{Z}[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ is a polynomial with integer coefficients in finitely many variables. Provide an algorithm (in the sense of a Turing machine, or equivalently a general recursive procedure) that takes as input an arbitrary such polynomial $P$ and outputs, in finitely many steps, "YES" if there exist integers $a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $P(a_1, \dots, a_n) = 0$, and "NO" otherwise. Equivalently: decide whether the set of polynomials $P \in \mathbb{Z}[x_1, x_2, \dots]$ admitting at least one integer zero is a recursive (decidable) subset of $\mathbb{Z}[x_1, x_2, \dots]$.
artifact.status_search_result: This is Hilbert's tenth problem. It was solved negatively: building on work of Davis, Putnam, and Robinson, Yuri Matiyasevich proved in 1970 (the MRDP theorem) that no such algorithm exists, since every recursively enumerable set is Diophantine.

status_evidence.title: Hilbert's tenth problem - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Matiyasevich's theorem, proved in 1970, states that no such algorithm exists.
status_evidence.claim: Hilbert's 10th problem was shown to be undecidable in 1970.
